subject: religious-studies

moments.title: Aquinas writes the Five Ways
moments.body: Aquinas's Five Ways (Quinque Viae) appear in Summa Theologiae I.2.3, occupying about a page. 1: motion (unmoved mover). 2: causation (uncaused first cause). 3: contingency (necessary being). 4: degrees (greatest being). 5: design (intelligent designer).
moments.takeaway: Aquinas presented the Ways as gestures toward a more developed natural theology, not stand-alone proofs. Modern apologetic use often isolates them from their original setting.

moments.title: Modern critiques
moments.body: Hume's Dialogues (1779) critiques the design argument. Kant (1781) argues that pure reason cannot prove God's existence — the cosmological and design arguments illegitimately apply categories of experience beyond experience. Both shape modern philosophy of religion.
moments.takeaway: The 'natural theology' tradition was on the defensive in the 19th century — and substantially revived in the 20th.

moments.title: Cosmological argument revived
moments.body: William Lane Craig's Kalam cosmological argument (developed from medieval Islamic sources): the universe began to exist; whatever begins to exist has a cause; therefore the universe has a cause. The Big Bang cosmology is presented as supporting the kalam premise. Edward Feser defends classical Thomist versions.
moments.takeaway: Contemporary natural theology (Plantinga, Swinburne, Craig, Feser) remains active. Whether the arguments are persuasive depends on prior commitments.

now.title: Arguments under examination
now.body: The Five Ways remain on every A-level Religious Studies syllabus. Modern atheistic responses (Bertrand Russell, Richard Dawkins) and theistic defences (Craig, Plantinga) coexist. The question — does any argument prove God's existence? — has been continuously discussed for 800 years.
now.open_questions: Do classical arguments work? Critics argue Hume and Kant settled the matter; defenders argue modern modal logic and cosmology have revived the arguments. The debate isn't resolvable empirically.

reflection: A 13th-century page in the Summa generated more philosophical work than almost any other equivalent text. The Five Ways remain a touchstone for thinking about the relationship between rational inquiry and religious belief.
